To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the lack of the Toll‐like receptors (TLR)2 and 4 in mice protects against a fat‐mediatated impairment in insulin‐mediated activity in the brain, locomotion, as well as sleep architecture.
Toll‐like receptor 2 and 3 deficiency in mice protects from high‐fat diet‐induced impairment of brain activity and locomotion by an interleukin‐mediated mechanism.
TLR2/TLR4 deficiency protects against HFD‐indiated impairment in insulin action in the CNS, locomotor activity, and sleep architecture, and that this protection is mediated by IL‐6 and osteopenin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Toll-like receptor 2 and 3 (TLR2 and TLR3) in insulin signaling in the brain and their potential role in obesity, diabetes, and sleep disorders.
the role of Toll‐like receptors (TLR) and the immune system in obesity and insulin resistance and their impact on the brain.
the role of the innate immune system in the regulation of insulin action and the development of insulin resistance in the central nervous system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

TLR2/TLR4 deficiency protects mice from HFD‐mediated impairment of brain insulin action by IL‐6‐dependent and osteopontins‐dependent mechanisms, resulting in a more active and less sleep state during the day and a more sleep state during the night.
TLR4 is involved in the pathogenesis of obesity and type 2 diabetes.
the lack of TLR2/TLR4 protects mice from fat‐mediated impairments of insulin action and brain activity by an IL‐ 6/OPN‐dependent mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TLR4 and TLR2 are involved in insulin resistance and obesity and that this is mediated by the pro‐inflammatory cytokines IL‐6 and IL‐1beta.

TLR2/TLR4 deficiency protects mice from HFD‐mediated impairment of insulin action, brain, and cortical activity as well as sleep architecture and that these effects are mediated by the proinflammatory cytokine interleukin‐ 6 and its downstream effector osteopontin.
Toll‐like receptor 2 and 3 are involved in the development of type 2 diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Toll‐like receptors TLR2/TLR4 are involved in the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes and that they are a novel therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes.
the Toll‐like receptors (TLR) 2 and 3 are important in the development of type 2 diabetes and obesity.
the lack of the TLRs 2 and 3 protects mice from a high‐fat–mediated impairment in brain activity, locomotor activity, and sleep architecture.
